extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, rhetoric, and critical reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for detecting and classifying logical fallacies in arguments, especially fallacies of generalization, ratiocination, and confusion (ambiguity). Intended to help evaluate the correctness and force of reasoning and to avoid common argumentative errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: False Analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferring conclusions from an analogy when the resemblance lacks the essential point (e.g. analogy from physical bodies to bodies politic; comparing gold to corn/coals where the utility depends on scarcity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that in the two cases the same law is really operating; there must be a connexion by means of causation between the known resemblance and the inferred one. Beware of analogies that omit the essential circumstance on which the argument hinges — the analogy alone does not prove anything. Examples: Hooker's 'primum mobile' analogy is fallacious; Whately's gold vs. corn analogy fails because utility depends on scarcity for gold but not for corn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misuse of Metaphor (Metaphors are not proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating metaphors or figurative illustrations as if they were proofs rather than aids to apprehension; using a vivid metaphor to imply the truth of what it illustrates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept a metaphor as demonstration: it 'assumes the proposition which it is brought to prove.' A good metaphor can suggest a proof or point to grounds, but its applicability must be established. Examples: D'Alembert's 'eagle and serpent' metaphor suggests explanatory mechanisms but does not prove them; Bacon's river/works analogy fails because the causes differ (levity vs. worthlessness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Generalization from Bad Classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawing wide generalizations from a class formed by bringing together heterogeneous items under one name (e.g. treating many different phenomena as instances of a single vague term like 'humidum' or 'kinêsis').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid forming classes by loose abstraction from a few familiar cases; check that the class members share important, not merely nominal or trivial, properties. Example: ancient use of 'motion' to cover all change led to confused reasoning; Bacon's use of broad terms like 'wet' or 'heat' shows the danger of vague classing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erroneous Conversion of Propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mistakenly converting universal affirmatives or hypotheticals (e.g. assuming from 'All A are B' that 'All B are A', or from 'If A then B' that 'If B then A').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that simple conversion of 'All A are B' to 'All B are A' is generally invalid; the proper converse of a hypothetical is 'If not-B then not-A', not 'If B then A'. People often accept conclusions as proof of premises; be cautious about inferring antecedents from consequents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusing Contraries and Contradictories
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to distinguish contraries (which can both be false) from contradictories (exact opposites), leading to the error of treating the denial of a wrong as proof of a right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to logical opposition: two contrary propositions may both be false, so the falsity of one does not establish the truth of the other. For detection, force the argument into explicit propositional form to reveal the misstep.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicious Syllogism (Illicit Processes / Undistributed Middle / More Than Three Terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllogistic errors such as introducing more than three terms (including covert terms), having an undistributed middle term, or illicitly distributing terms (illicit process of extremes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the rules of the syllogism to expose these faults: formally set out premises to see suppressed links; syllogistic form helps to discover if the conclusion follows. Note that a reasoner can often save a conclusion by introducing a false premise, so demand explicit premises and check distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing the Premises (à dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a premise that is true only with a qualification as if it were absolutely true — dropping necessary limitations (time, conditions) when applying it to new circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for lost qualifications or omitted conditions when a previously established proposition is reused. Examples: Mercantile theory misapplies 'whatever brings in money enriches' without its provisos; arguments about tithes confuse conditional comparisons with unconditional conclusions; many political/economic errors arise from this fallacy. Frequently the omitted condition is a temporal one ('always find their level' misread as 'always at their level').

rubrics_metrics.name: Misapplication of Abstract Truths (Reasoning 'in the abstract' as Absolute)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating principles that are true 'in the abstract' (with all modifying causes absent) as if they held absolutely in real-world circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify modifying causes and limiting conditions before applying abstract principles to practice. The common error is to ignore circumstances that the abstract statement assumed away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Ambiguity / Equivocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors arising from ambiguous use of terms: when something true under one sense of a word is reasoned on as if true under another sense (including ambiguous middle terms or shifting senses between premises and conclusion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect ambiguous middle terms and shifts of sense by pinning down definitions in each premise and the conclusion. Be alert to 'paronymous' or conjugate words treated as if they had identical meanings (e.g. 'project' vs. 'projector'), and to fallacies built on grammatical affinities. Force terms to be used consistently throughout the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacy Founded on Etymology
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguing from a term's etymological or original sense rather than its customary legal or practical meaning (e.g. 'representative' ought to correspond strictly to the verb 'represent').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer law, custom, and current usage to etymological prescripts when interpreting terms in practical or political contexts; check how the term functions in practice rather than its linguistic roots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguous Political/Economic Expressions (practical equivocations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific recurring ambiguities that mislead public reasoning: e.g. 'scarcity of money' (currency vs. capital seeking investment), 'influence of property' (persuasive vs. coercive influence), 'theory' (proper scientific generalization vs. mere speculation), and 'the Church' (clergy vs. whole body of believers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify which sense is intended before drawing inferences; analyze the distinct senses and their relevant consequences. These ambiguities often sit 'on the threshold' of a subject and must be resolved to avoid systematic error.
